value: Here the resistance is a third branch across the coil and capacitor. At resonance their currents are equal and opposite, so together they draw no net current from the source; only the resistance does, so the impedance is about R, the circuit's maximum.
reason: The old explanation never said why the key is R rather than something higher. NEETS Module 9 p. 1-22: at resonance the branch currents are equal and opposite and the circuit has maximum impedance.

value: B: the reactive branch currents cancel, so the inductive reactance does not set the impedance. C: at resonance the coil and capacitor draw no net current, so nothing pulls the impedance below R. D: with the reactive branches drawing no net current, the resistance alone sets the impedance, so it cannot rise above R.
reason: The old D line ('the pool's answer is that it is about equal to the resistance') was circular and explained nothing.

value: In a parallel circuit the resistance is a branch across the tank: the higher it is, the less current it wastes and the lower the loss, so Q rises with R. Hence Q = R ÷ X, using either reactance, since XL equals XC at resonance; the series form is X ÷ R.
reason: The old explanation gave the rule as 'the pool's rule' without saying why R goes on top. NEETS Module 9 p. 1-28: 'high power loss is low Q; low power loss is high Q.'

value: B and C: 23.5 kHz and 7.12 kHz are hundreds to a thousand times too low; microhenries and picofarads resonate in the megahertz range. D: 23.5 MHz does not come from the formula, which gives 7.12 MHz.
reason: The old line said both kilohertz answers are 'a thousand or more times too low', but 7.12 MHz ÷ 23.5 kHz is only about 300.

value: Symbols 4 and 5 are the dual-gate MOSFETs, each with two gates. In FET symbols the arrow points towards N-type material, so symbol 4's arrow, pointing into the channel, marks the N-channel device.
reason: The old explanation said only that 'the pool keys symbol 4', which does not tell 4 from 5. NEETS Module 7 p. 3-39: 'the arrow in a JFET symbol always points towards the N-type material', as in transistor symbols.

value: A: symbol 2 has a single gate. C: symbol 5 is the other dual-gate MOSFET, but its arrow points away from the channel, marking P-channel. D: symbol 6 has one gate joined to the channel, a junction FET.
reason: Says why symbol 5, the close trap, is wrong.

value: Symbols 1 and 6 are junction FETs, with the gate joined straight to the channel. The arrow points towards N-type material, so in a P-channel JFET it points away from the channel towards the gate, as in symbol 1.
reason: The old explanation said only that 'the pool keys it'. NEETS Module 7 p. 3-39: 'the P-channel symbol shows the arrow pointing away from the drain/source channel toward the gate.'

value: B and C: symbols 2 and 3 are single-gate MOSFETs, with the gate set apart from the channel. D: symbol 6's arrow points into the channel, marking an N-channel JFET.
reason: Says what the reversed arrow on symbol 6 means.

value: A Schottky diode is drawn with its cathode bar ending in two hooks, like a squared-off letter S. Symbol 6 is the only one drawn that way.
reason: The old explanation said only that the pool keys symbol 6, giving no way to recognise the symbol.

value: A: symbol 1 has a curved bar. C: symbol 2 has two diodes back to back. D: symbol 3's bar has slanted ends like a letter Z, not hooks.
reason: Figure E6-2 shows symbol 3's bar bent at both ends, not 'at one end only'.

value: Brass is a non-magnetic conductor. The coil's changing field induces currents in it that set up an opposing field, reducing the total field and so the inductance. Ferrite, a magnetic material, raises it instead.
reason: The old explanation just said the pool gives brass. NEETS Module 11 p. 1-50: a nonmagnetic slug has current induced in it 'that sets up an opposing H field' which 'reduces the total inductance'.

value: A: ceramic neither conducts nor is magnetic, so it sets up no opposing field. C: ferrite is magnetic and raises inductance. D: aluminium is also a non-magnetic conductor and would lower inductance the same way, but the pool keys brass.
reason: The old D line ('not the pool's answer') hid that aluminium works by the same mechanism as brass; the card should say so honestly.

value: Light is a form of energy that electrons can absorb. With enough of it an electron breaks free of its bond and can carry current, which is how the cell turns light into electrical energy.
reason: The old explanation just said 'in the pool's answer the electrons take up the light's energy'. NEETS Module 7 p. 1-8: the energy to move an electron 'can be in the form of electric fields, heat, light'; p. 1-12: absorbed energy breaks covalent bonds, freeing electrons.

value: A: protons stay in the nucleus; it is the outer electrons that take up energy. B: photons are the light arriving, not what absorbs it. D: a hole is the gap an electron leaves, not what absorbs the energy.
reason: The old A and D lines said only 'not the pool's answer'. NEETS Module 7 p. 1-12 defines the hole as the vacancy left by a missing valence electron.

value: In a semiconductor crystal, energy absorbed from light lets valence electrons break their covalent bonds and move into the conduction band, so the more light, the lower the resistance.
reason: The old explanation restated the pool. NEETS Module 7 p. 1-12: absorbed energy lets valence electrons break covalent bonds and move to the conduction band, where they support current.

value: Equal resistors across capacitors in series divide the voltage equally between them, give the stored charge a path to drain away after switch-off, and draw a small steady current that acts as a minimum load.
reason: The old explanation said only that 'the pool credits these resistors with all three jobs', not how each comes about.

'Thicker than a thin one of the same size' is confusing (same physical length is meant), and the card never says why a thicker conductor is electrically longer. No saved source states the reason; NEETS Module 10 notes only that diameter 'has an effect on tuning'.
The explanation restates the pool ('higher electron mobility is the property the pool gives') and never says what electron mobility is or why it helps at UHF. No saved source defines it.
'The three silicon-based options all fall short' gives no reason why GaN reaches the highest frequency. No saved source covers GaN.
The explanation restates the key. It should say that a DIP's pins pass through holes in the board, while PLCC, BGA and SOT are soldered to the surface; no saved source states this.
'Silicon is the pool's answer' explains nothing. NEETS Module 7 p. 1-2 says only that silicon was 'the most stable of the materials tested', which does not cover solar cells.
The primer never says what electron mobility is (how readily electrons move through a material under a voltage). The card cites only E6E01, which does not define it.
The back never defines through-hole (leads pass through holes in the board and are soldered on the far side); only the example hints at it. E6E02 does not define it.

The back never says what an RF choke is. NEETS Module 7 p. 3-17 (#page=131) could support a definition: the radio-frequency choke 'provides high inductive reactance at the tank frequency to prevent tank loading'. That needs a change of source, or a second source, on the card.
